la:adj:pius.html:
pĭus (written PIIVS, Inscr. Viscont. Monum. Degli Scip. tab. 6, n. 1; cf. ), a, um (voc. pie:
o crucifer bone, lucisator Omnipotens pie,.—Comp. only magis pius; cf. Charis. pp. 88 and 130 P.—Sup.: piissimus, used by Antonius, and condemned by Cicero, as: verbum omnino nullum in linguā Latinā,; but freq. in the post-Aug. per., e. g. ; ; ; ; ; et saep. From rare form PIENS, found in inscriptions, Murat. 1624, 4; Mus. Ver. 129, 3 Maff., is derived another form of the sup., PIENTISSIMVS, ; ; ), adj.
etym. dub.; often referred to τίω, τιμάω
, that acts according to duty, dutiful; esp. that performs what is due to the gods and religion in general, to parrents, kindred, teachers, country; pious, devout, conscientious, affectionate, tender, kind, good, grateful, respectful, loyal, patriotic, etc. (of persons and things): si quis pius est,: uxor pia et pudica,: Capus ... pium ex se Anchisen generat, Enn. ap. Philarg. ad (Ann. v. 31 Vahl.): (deos) piorum et impiorum habere rationem,; : di meliora piis,: poëta,: pii vates. ; cf.: pio vatis ab ore,.—So as subst. freq. pĭi, of the departed, the blessed: piorum sedes,: arva piorum,: cf. Bentley on .—Of things having reference to religion: far,: tura,; : luci,sacred, holy,: pia et aeterna pax,a conscientiously kept and eternal peace,: Poeni homines immolare pium esse duxerunt,; cf. : ore pio,; so, quosque pium est adhibere deos,.— As subst.: pĭum, i, n.: stabit pro signis jusque piumque tuis,justice and equity,; .—Of respectful, affectionate conduct towards parents, etc.: pius in parentes,: pius Aeneas, on account of his filial love for Anchises,; ; ; 4, 393; 5, 26 et saep.; cf.: seniorque parens, pia sarcina nati,; : pius dolor,: impietate pia est, she is affectionate (towards her brothers) through want of affection (for her son), her sisterly triumphed over her maternal love, : quo pius affectu Castora frater amat,: metus,of a wife for her husband,: bellum, waged for one's country or allies, ; ; .—
Transf., in gen.
Honest, upright, honorable (very rare): pius quaestus, Cato, R. R. praef.—
Benevolent, kind, gentle, gracious (postAug.): clementia patrem tuum in primis Pii nomine ornavit, M. Aurel. ap. Vulcat. Gallic. in Avid. Cass. 11: pius enim et clemens es, Dominus Deus,; .—Pĭus, a title of the emperors after M. Antoninus, on coins and inscrr.; v. Eckh. D. N. 7, p. 36; 8, p. 453; —Poet., of a wine-jar: testa, my kindly jar, = benigna, .—Hence, adv.: pĭē, piously, religiously, dutifully, affectionately: pie sancteque colere deos,; ; : memoriam nostri pie inviolateque servabitis,: metuo ne scelerate dicam in te, quod pro Milone dicam pie,: pie lugere,; .—Sup.: quod utrumque piissime tulit,.

la:noun:pietas.gloss: dutiful conduct, sense of duty and responsibility
senses: dutiful conduct, sense of duty and responsibility
duty, dutifulness, affection, love, loyalty, patriotism, gratitude
la:noun:pietas.html:
pĭĕtas, ātis, f.
pius
,
dutiful conduct towards the gods, one's parents, relatives, benefactors, country, etc., sense of duty.
Lit.
With respect to the gods, piety: est enim pietas justitia adversus deos,; ; cf.: aequitas tripartita dicitur esse; una ad superos deos, altera ad manes, tertia ad homines pertinere. Prima pietas, secunda sanctitas, tertia justitia aut aequitas nominatur,: pietas adversus deos, id.

Fin. 3, 22, 73: deos placatos pietas efficiet et sanctitas,; : senex fretus pietate deum,; Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 369 Vahl.): nec pietas ulla est, velatum saepe videri Vortier ad lapidem atque omnes accedere ad aras, etc., that is not piety, to incline with veiled head to the marble, etc., .—

Conscientiousness, scrupulousness, .—So of love and duty towards God (eccl. Lat.; freq.),; Pet. 1, 6.—Plur., Pet. 3, 11.—
With respect to one's parents, children, relatives, country, benefactors, etc., duty, dutifulness, affection, love, loyalty, patriotism, gratitude, etc.: Pa. Salve, mi pater insperate. Tr. Volup est, quom istuc ex pietate vestrā nobis contigit, : patrem tuom si percoles per pietatem,dutifully,: justitia erga deos religio, erga parentes pietas nominatur,: quid est pietas, nisi voluntas grata in parentes?: justitiam cole et pietatem, quae cum sit magna in parentibus et propinquis, tum in patriā maxima est,; cf.: pietas, quae erga patriam aut parentes, aut alios sanguine conjunctos officium conservare monet,; : pietas in matrem,; : mi mater, tua pietas plane nobis auxilio fuit,; cf. v. 99: felix nati pietate,: solemnia pietatis,the last offices,: egregium narras mirā pietate parentem,: pietas erga aliquem,: in aliquem,: hic tui omnes valent summāque pietate te desiderant,: nec publicae pietatis intererat, quid vocarere,to the affection of the citizens,: militiae,.—Towards a husband (rare): neque id (officium nostrum) magis facimus quam nos monet pietas,; cf.: scelus est pietas in conjuge Tereo,.—The formula PIETATIS CAVSA or EX PIETATE (opp. EX TESTAMENTO), in epitaphs, denotes that the heir raised the monument to the deceased, not because compelled by the latter's last will, but out of affection and respect, ; , n. 314.—
Transf., in gen. (mostly poet. and in postAug. prose).
Justice: at tibi ... pro talibus ausis Di, si qua est caelo pietas, quae talia curet, Persolvant grates dignas, etc.,; cf. ; so : summa deum pietas,; cf. .—
Gentleness, kindness, tenderness, pity, compassion: permittite Patres Conscripti a pietate vestrā impetrari, ut damnatis liberum mortis arbitrium indulgeatis,: senatus,; .—In addressing a person: mea pietas,my kind friend,.—
Pĭĕtas, personified, a goddess, Piety, who had two temples at Rome, ; ; ; ; ; ; Müll.; ; .

la:noun:pigritia.html:
pī^grĭtĭa, ae, and pī^grĭtĭes, ēi, f.
id.
,
sloth, sluggishness, laziness, indolence (cf.: desidia, socordia, inertia, segnities).
Lit.: pigritiam definiunt metum consequentis laboris,: propter pigritiam aut ignaviam,: noli putare pigritiā me facere, quod non meā manu scribam,: et haesitatio, : nox Romanis pigritiem ad sequendum fecit,: lentae crimine pigritiae,.—
Transf.
Tu das ingenuae jus mihi pigritiae, honorable repose, leisure, .—
Stomachi, weakness of the stomach, .

la:verb:pingo.html:
pingo, pinxi, pictum, 3, v. a.,
to represent pictorially with the pencil or needle, to paint, embroider (cf.: depingo, delineo, adumbro).
Lit.: quas (comas) Dione Pingitur sustinuisse manu,is represented in painting,; : tabulas,: tabula picta,a painting, picture,: pingere hominis speciem,: Helenae simulacrum,: Nero princeps jusserat colosseum se pingi,.—Prov.: quae dicunt ii, qui numquam philosophum pictum, ut dicitur, viderunt, of those who speak of things they know nothing about,.— Of embroidering (with or without acu): textile stragulum, magnificis operibus pictum,: pingere acu,: picti reges,in embroidered garments,: picti tori,with embroidered coverlets,: toga,the embroidered toga worn by a triumphing commander,: tapetes,.—Pass. in mid. force: pingi,to paint the face,.—
Transf.
To paint, stain, color with any thing (mostly poet.): palloribus omnia pingunt,; : sanguineis frontem moris et tempora pingit,; ; : multas facies,: oculos,; so, oculos stibio,. —Esp., to tattoo: Agathyrsi ora artusque pingunt iisdem omnes notis, et sic ut ablui nequeunt,: membraque qui ferro gaudet pinxisse Gelonus,.—
To adorn, decorate, embellish: herbas floribus,: bibliothecam aliquā re,: stellis pingitur aether,.—
Trop., of style, to paint, color, embellish: verba,: tabula, quam Cleanthes sane commode verbis depingere solebat,: locus, quem ego varie meis orationibus soleo pingere,: modo mihi date Britanniam, quam pingam coloribus tuis penicillo meo,, a, 2: hunc (virum) omnibus a me pictum et politum artis coloribus subito deformatum vidi,.—Hence, pictus, a, um, P. a., painted, colored, of various colors.
Lit.: volucres,: pelles,: absint et picti squalentia terga lacerti,: puppes,: carinae,.—
Transf., tattooed: Geloni,: Agathyrsi, Forbig. ad loc.; .—
Of style, ornamented, ornate: orationis pictum et expolitum genus, 27, 96: Lysiā nihil potest esse pictius,.—
Merely painted, i. e. unreal, false, deceptive, empty, vain: pictos experiere metus,

la:verb:pio.html:
pĭo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
pius

To seek to appease, to appease, propitiate by sacrifice (syn. place).—
Lit.: Silvanum lacte piabant,: ossa,: busta (i.e. Manes),: Janus Agonali luce piandus erit,.—
Transf.
To honor with religious rites, to celebrate: ubi piem Pietatem,: aras ture, (4, 9), 19: in magicis astra piare focis,to perform sacred rites,.—
To purify with sacred rites (syn.: procuro, lustro): si quid tibi piandum fuisset,.—
To make or seek to make good, to atone for, expiate: damna,: mors morte pianda est,: fulmen,to avert by sacrifice the misfortune portended by lightning,: nefas triste,to atone for, avert the penalty,; : cometes terrificum sidus, ac non leviter piatum,.—
To punish, avenge: culpam morte,: grande nefas et morte piandum,.—
To free from madness, Müll.: jube te piari de meā pecuniā: nam ego quidem insanum te esse certo scio,; so .

pīla, ae, f.

senses: a heavy javelin, throwing spear, of the Roman soldier
la:noun:pilum.html:
pīlum, i, n.
for pis-lum, cf. piso, 1. pila, etc.
,
a pounder, pestle of a mortar.
Lit.: pilum fabarium,; : quasi tollenonem aut pilum Graecum reciproces planā viā, a pounder, in using which, one side was raised while the other was depressed, Plaut. Fragm. ap. Fest. s v. reciprocare, p. 274 Müll.: pinsente pilo praeferrato,: pilo contusum,.—
Transf., the heavy javelin of the Roman infantry, which they hurled at the enemy at the commencement of the action, and then took to their swords: (caput) adfixum gestari jussit in pilo,: pilum, haud paulo quam hasta, vehementius ictu missuque telum,; cf. : milites e loco superiore pilis missis facile hostium phalangem perfregerunt,: pilorum hastarumque honore circumdatus,: in imperatorem suum legiones pila torserunt,; cf. : pilum praepilatum, having a blunt or rounded end, Auct. B. Afr. 72. They were also used in sieges, being hurled at the enemy from the walls; these were called pila muralia,; .—Prov.: pilum inicere alicui,to make an attack on one,.—
Vis certe pila, i. e. to be primipilus of the triarii or veterans who carried two javelins each, ; v. Dict. of Antiq. p. 104.

la:verb:pilo.html:
pīlo, no
perf., ātum, 1, v. a., = πιλέω, qs. to ram down; hence, in gen., to thrust home (ante-class. and rare): hastam pilans prae pondere frangit, Host. ap. (pilans id est figens, Serv.). —Hence, pīlātus, a, um, P. a., closepressed, thick, dense = densus, pressus.
Lit.: pilatum (agmen), quod sine jumentis incedit, sed inter se densum est, quo facilius per iniquiora loca tramittatur, Varr. ap. : inde loci liquidas pilatasque aetheris oras Contemplor, Enn. ib. (firmas et stabiles significat et quasi pilis fultas, Serv.; cf. Vahl.).—
Trop.: sententia praesto pectore pilata, Hostius ap. (id est fixa, Serv.).

senses: to rob (attested from ca. 400 CE; cf. the similar sense of compīlō)

la:noun:pictura.html:
pictūra, ae, f.
pingo
,
painting, the art of painting.
Lit.: una est ars ratioque picturae,; ; ; .—
In partic., a painting of the face, .—
Transf., concr., a painting, picture (cf. tabula): et si qua inutilis pictura sit, eam vendat,; : nego ullam picturam neque in tabulis neque textilem fuisse, quin conquisierit, : accedant statuae et picturae,: positae sunt picturae Herculis liberos occidentis,: statuas et picturas avehere,: dicitur tabulam picturae cedere,.—Of embroideries: textilibus picturis,.—Of paintings in Mosaic, .—Of a carving in relief: et sculpsit in eis picturam cherubim,.—
Trop., a painting, picture in words: animum ab istā picturā imaginibusque virtutum traducere,: Homerum tradunt caecum fuisse; at ejus picturam, non poësin videmus,.

la:adj:pinguis.html:
pinguis, e, adj.
root pag-, pak-, of pango, q. v.; cf. Gr. παχύς, stout
, = πίων,
fat (opp. macer; syn.: opimus, obesus).
Lit.: pingues Thebani,: pingui tentus omaso Furius,: me pinguem et nitidum bene curatā cute vises,: Lateranus,: pinguem facere gallinam,: pinguior agnus,: pinguissimus haedulus,: merum, rich, oily wine (= plenum), .— Subst.: pingue, is, n., fat, grease, ; : taurorum, leonum ac pantherarum pinguia,: comedite pinguia, Esd. 8, 10.—
Transf.
Pass., fat, rich, fertile; also, plump, in good condition: ager,; ; cf.: sanguine pinguior Campus,: sulcus,i. e. drawn in a rich soil,: fimus,: hortus,: stabula, of beehives,rich, full of honey,: arae,: ficus,plump, juicy,; cf. saliva,: flamma, of incense; tura pingues facientia flammas,: corpora suco pinguis olivae Splendescunt,: pingues taedae,full of pitch,: pingues arae,full of fat and blood,: coma,anointed, (different from ; v.infra 3): mensa,rich, luxurious,; cf.: incusa pingui auro dona,. —Of color, dull, faint, . —Act., that makes fat; hence, meton., fertilizing: pingui flumine Nilus,.—
Bedaubed, besmeared: pinguia crura luto,: virga,limed twigs,.—
Thick, dense: caelum pingue et concretum (opp. caelum tenue et purum),: folia pinguissima,: toga,: lacernae,: pinguissima coma,very thick, luxuriant hair,.—
Of taste, dull, insipid, not sharp, not pungent: sapor,; .—
Trop.
Of the mind, dull, gross, heavy, stupid, doltish: Cordubae natis poëtis pingue quiddam sonantibus et peregrinum,: pingue videbatur et sibi contrarium,: nec prave factis decorari versibus opto, Ne rubeam pingui donatus munere,: pingue sed ingenium mansit,: insubidius nescio quid facies et pinguius, (20), 4: pinguis Minerva, v. Minerva.—
Siout, bold, strong: verba,: facundia,.—
Calm, quiet, comfortable, easy (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): et pingui membra quiete levat,; : amor,: secessus,: mollem in posterum et pinguem destinare vitam,: pinguius otium,.—
Sleek, spruce, trim, = nitidus: pexus pinguisque doctor, Spald.— Hence, adv.: pinguĭter.
Lit., fatly, with fatness, .—
Transf., abundantly, liberally: pinguius succurrere,.—
Trop., dully, stupidly: pinguius aliquid accipere,.

pīnĕus, a, um, adj.
id.
,
of the pine, piny, pine-: pinea velamina,pine-wreaths,: ardor,a fire of pine-wood,: silva,: plaga pinea,a piny tract,: claustra,i. e. of the wooden horse before Troy,: fert avidas in pinea Turnus Texta faces,i. e. into the ships,; so, pinea moles,a ship,compages,: nuclei,; : nuces,.—

pix

la:noun:pignus.html:
pignus, ŏris and ĕris (old form in plur.:
pignosa pignora eodem modo quo valesii, auselii ... dicebantur, Müll.), n.
root pac-, of pango; cf. paciscor
, a pledge, gage, pawn, security, mortgage (of persons as well as things).
Lit.: opponere se pigneri,: ager oppositus est pignori,: servus, quem hic reliqueram Pignus pro me,: quo facto pignore animos centurionum devinxit,: rem alicujus pignori accipere,: pignora apud se deposita persequi et vindicare,: sub pignoribus mutuas pecunias accipere,: habere aliquid pignori,: liberare pignus a creditore,: pignoribus cavere alicui,: aurum

pignori apud aliquem ponere, : viginti milia faenus pignoribus positis,income from mortgages,.—Esp., of the security for the payment of his fine, which was taken by the consul of a senator who failed to attend in the Senate: pignus auferre,: pignoribus terreri, Crass. ib.; so, senatores pignoribus cogere,: pignora capere,; of hostages,: marium pignora,male hostages,: pignus praetorium, the security which the prœtor took as a guarantee for the preservation of a thing when he put it in the possession of a creditor, or fidei commissarius, ; .—

Esp., in phrases.
Pignus capere, to take a pledge or security for payment: certis verbis pignus capiebatur,; —
Pignora capere, to issue execution, make seizure of property: Vettium, pignoribus captis, cojecit in carcerem,: eorum, qui debita confessi sunt, pignora capi et distrahi possunt, A, 4: per vim debitoris sui pignora, cum non haberet obligata, capere,.—
Pignoris capio, a proceeding by which the summary collection of certain debts was secured, (v. Sandars ad introd. § 96).—
Transf.

Children, parents, brothers and sisters, relatives, as pledges of love (only after the Aug. period): nunc tibi commendo communia pignora, natos, : prolemque gemellam Pignora bina dedi,: tot natos natasque et pignora cara nepotes,: ascita pignora,: pignora conjugum ac liberorum,: obsecratio illa judicum, per carissima pignora, utique, si et reo sint liberi, conjux, parentes, utilis erit,: habens filiam, uxorem, nepotem, sorores, interque tot pignora veros amicos,; : proxima pignora,: ne in conjugem, in familiam, in cetera pignora ejus saeviret,; : frangi aspectu pignorum suorum,.—Hence, in gen.,

la:verb:pigeo.html:
pĭgĕo, gŭi, and pĭgĭtum est, 2, v. a.
root pik-, to be angry; cf.: peccare, pejor (for pec-ior), pessimus (contr. from pējessimus); Gr. πικρός, bitter
,
to feel annoyance or reluctance at; to repent of a thing.
As a verb. pers. (very rare): pudet quod turpe est; piget quod dolet, Donat. ap. : poscis ab invitā verba pigenda lyra,.—
Piget, piguit, or pigitum est, third pers. sing. impers., it irks, troubles, displeases, chagrins, afflicts, grieves, disgusts one; I (thou, he, etc.), dislike, loathe, etc.; with acc. of the person and gen. of the thing; with inf.; with acc. and inf.; with two acc.; absol., etc. (cf. taedet).—With acc. and gen.: mea mater, tui me miseret, mei piget, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 82): dolet pudetque Graium me et vero piget, id. ap. : hortari pudet, non prodesse id piget,: pudet pigetque mei me, : fratris me quidem Piget pudetque,: dum me civitatis morum piget taedetque,.—With subject-clause: non dedisse ipsum pudet; me, quia non accepi, piget,: nisi forte pudet aut piget recte facere, Sall. Or. contr. Lep. med.: nam postea quae fecerit incertum habeo, pudeat magis an pigeat disserere,: longos castrorum ferre dolores si piget,: neque enim me piguit quaerere,: ut Silanum non piguerit sententiam suam interpretatione lenire,: nec pigitum parvos lares ... subire,; Auct. ap. : non te pigeat visitare infirmum,.—With neutr. pron.: illud quod piget,: factum id esse non negat, Neque se id pigere,.—Absol.: oratione multitudo ad misericordiam inducitur, ad pudendum, ad pigendum,.—
Transf.

It makes one ashamed; I (thou, he, etc.) am ashamed: fateri pigebat,; .

the name of a Roman sacerdotal family. la:noun:pistrinum.html:
pistrīnum (pristrīnum, Ritschl; Fleck.), i, n.
pistor
,
a place where corn is pounded, a pounding-mill, mill; usually worked by horses or asses; but sometimes a lazy or otherwise bad slave was forced to perform this labor (cf. mola).
Lit.: ut ferratus in pistrino aetatem conteras,: in pistrinum tradi,: in pristrino credo, ut convenit fore,: te in pistrinum, Dave, dedam usque ad necem,: oratorem in judicium, tamquam in aliquod pistrinum, detrudi et compingi videbam,; .—As a term of reproach, of bad slaves: pristrinorum civitas,.—
Transf.
Because bread was usually baked at the mill, a bakery: exercere pistrinum,: aliquem in pistrinum submittere,; swine were fed there upon the bran,.—
A wearisome, oppressive labor, drudgery: tibi mecum in eodem est pistrino, Crasse, vivendum,.

la:verb:pignero.html:
pignĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
pignus
,

Lit.: unionem,: bona tantum, quae publicari poterant, pigneranda poenae praebebant, furnished as security for the penalty, i. e. left to be confiscated, : cujus et alveolos et laenam pignerat Atreus,which the poet Rubrenus, while he was writing the Atreus, was compelled by necessity to pawn,: ancilla pignerata,: vestimenta pignorata,.—
Trop.
To pledge one's life, etc.: velut obsidibus datis pigneratos habere animos,.—
To bind a person or thing to one's self, to make one's own: pignerare aliquem sibi beneficio,: optimates viros curiae suae, Naz. Pan. ad Const. 35.—With se, to pledge one's self: se cenae alicujus,to promise to dine with one,; , p. 269, 25.

la:other:Pinarius.html:
Pīnārĭus, i, m.,
the name of a Roman sacerdotal family. The Pinarii and Potitii presided at the celebration of certain sacred rites in honor of Hercules, originally instituted by Evander and re-established by Romulus. The Pinarii having on one occasion arrived after the exta were consumed, it was ordained that, as long as the family remained, they should not partake of the exta, sqq.; 9, 29, 9 sqq.; ; Müll. —Hence, Pīnārĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Pinarii, Pinarian: Pinaria domus,: Pinaria gens,: Pinaria tribus, Fest. s. v. popilia, p. 233 Müll.
